name: Fresco — the scribe for construction superintendents
contextUnderstands: Construction superintendents at general contractors who keep an accurate record of work on site, when site walks are done and photos and notes go into the log, counting the last 5 working days.

vectors.statement: Construction superintendents at general contractors walk their sites and take photos all day. Once the walks are done, they sit in the trailer sorting and uploading those photos and typing up daily logs and punch lists. It eats a large part of the day, often after everyone else has left. They do it mostly to protect themselves if the owner disputes the work or a liability claim comes up, so they keep doing it by hand.

people.followUp: Schedule and keeping my guys safe. The logs get done one way or another.
My log's done on the tablet before I leave the gate. Keeping the schedule and getting subs to show up is what eats my day.

Safety and the schedule are the job. The log takes me forty minutes and I'd rather write it myself anyway, it's my name on it.
My assistant super writes the log, so it's not on my plate. Chasing RFIs and holding the schedule is.

vectors.statement: When the site walk is happening and the superintendent wants to capture what they see and say, the construction superintendent takes short videos during the walk and talks over them, and the tool turns them into notes with photos, assignees and due dates, texts the crew their action items, and sends the notes to the project system on one click and gets back written site notes with photos, assignees and due dates, and a text with action items sent to each crew member.

people.followUp: We already pay for project software on every job. A second fee per site that size is hard to justify when the logs get done either way.
Our supers don't lose much time on logs, so there's nothing to pay it out of. It's a nice extra, not a cost we carry.
I wouldn't put money on an app writing our legal record. If the notes are wrong in a dispute, that's on us, not the vendor.
I can't tell you what the logs cost us now, so I can't justify a thousand a site. Show me the hours first.
Across all our jobs a per-site fee adds up fast. If it were priced by the supers actually using it, I'd go higher.
Cleaning up logs costs us about six hundred a month in overtime today, so paying more than that to fix it makes no sense.
